blocks.prompt: The Heaviest Hat in the World
blocks.text: A real crown is heavier than it looks. The crown used to crown a king of England is called St Edward's Crown. It is made of solid gold. It has 444 stones on it. It weighs about as much as a house brick. The king wears it for only a few minutes. Then he takes it off and puts on a lighter one for the rest of the day. When nobody is wearing it, the crown lives in a stone castle called the Tower of London. It sits behind thick glass. Guards watch it all night. Anyone can go and look at it, but nobody can touch it.

blocks.prompt: Why Crowns Are Made of Gold
blocks.text: Crowns could be made of iron. Iron is strong and it is cheap. But leave iron out in the rain and it turns orange and flaky. Silver is beautiful, but silver goes black and dull and has to be polished over and over. Gold does neither. Gold does not rust. Divers pull gold coins out of shipwrecks that sank hundreds of years ago, and the gold comes up as bright as the day it went down. That is the first reason crowns are gold. The second reason is that gold is soft. A goldsmith can hammer it thin, bend it, and curl it into points and arches without much of a fight. Try that with iron and you need a roaring fire and a heavy hammer. The third reason is that gold is rare. Anyone can find a rock. Almost nobody finds gold. A thing that is hard to get says something about the person wearing it. Gold does have one problem. It is heavy. St Edward's Crown, used to crown a British king, weighs about as much as a house brick. Kings wear it for a few minutes, then swap it for something lighter.

notes: The Black Prince's Ruby is not a ruby

It sits in the Imperial State Crown

blocks.prompt: The Red Stone That Is Not a Ruby
blocks.text: Near the front of the Imperial State Crown, just above the band, sits a red stone about the size of a small hen's egg. It is called the Black Prince's Ruby, and it has belonged to the crown jewels of England for more than six hundred years. According to the traditional story, it was handed to Edward of Woodstock, the prince they called the Black Prince, in 1367, and Henry V is said to have worn it on his helmet at the battle of Agincourt in 1415. There is one problem with the name. It is not a ruby. It is a spinel. For most of history nobody could have known that, because a ruby and a red spinel look almost identical. Both are hard. Both are glassy. Both get their red from tiny traces of a metal called chromium. If you found either one lying in a stream, you would call it a ruby and feel certain. Underneath, they are different minerals. A ruby is corundum, made of aluminum and oxygen. A spinel adds magnesium, and its atoms stack in a different pattern. That hidden pattern changes what light does inside the stone. Light passing through a ruby splits into two beams. Light passing through a spinel does not. Once gemologists learned to test for that split, the great red stones of Europe began failing one after another. The Black Prince's Ruby failed. So did the Timur Ruby, another famous red stone in the same royal collection. Nothing about the stone itself changed. It is exactly as old, as red, and as rare as it was before. The only thing that changed was how much we knew, which is usually what happens when a fact gets corrected.

answers: it is a spinel, which adds magnesium and stacks its atoms differently than corundum
light splits into two beams inside a ruby but not inside a spinel

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A plain band is called a circlet
Arches over the top mean nobody ranks above you
The globe and cross on top is called the monde
Parliament melted the English regalia in 1649
The Coronation Spoon survived and dates from the 1100s
Most of the Crown Jewels were remade in 1661

blocks.prompt: What the Shape of a Crown Is Saying
blocks.text: A crown is not jewelry. It is a sentence, written in gold, and every part of it means something. Start with the simplest crown: a plain band that goes around the head. A circlet. It says the wearer is important, and it stops there. For centuries that was enough for most European kings, because most European kings were not entirely their own masters. Above them sat emperors, and above everyone sat the Pope. A ring of gold made a modest claim, and the modest claim was accurate. Then crowns grew arches. Bands of gold rise from the circlet, cross over the top of the head, and meet in the middle, where they carry a small globe and a cross. This is called a closed crown, and the arches are not decoration. Closing the top was a way of announcing that nothing sat above the wearer. English kings took up the arched crown around the reigns of Henry VII and Henry VIII, at exactly the point when England was insisting that it answered to no foreign power. The argument was in the law, and it was also in the metal. If a crown can make a claim, the claim can be refused. In 1649, after the English Civil War, Parliament executed King Charles I and then went after his crowns. The regalia was carried out of Westminster Abbey, broken apart, and melted down. The gold became coins. The stones were weighed and sold off like scrap metal. The money raised was not the point, because it was not very much money. The point was that the objects were claims, and the claims were being denied. Almost nothing survived. One piece that did was the Coronation Spoon, a plain silver-gilt spoon made in the 1100s, which is now the oldest object in the British Crown Jewels. Eleven years later the monarchy came back, and the whole set had to be built again from nothing. That is why crowns that look ancient were mostly made in 1661. The claim returned. The metal was new.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Rome's highest honor was a crown of grass
The civic crown was oak leaves, for saving a life
No pharaoh's crown has ever been found
Arches on a crown claim sovereignty
The English regalia was melted in 1649
The Koh-i-Noor is 105.6 carats and still contested

blocks.prompt: Arguments Made of Gold
blocks.text: We think we know what a crown is: gold, jewels, heavy, expensive. The most valuable crown in Roman history was made of grass. It was called the corona graminea, the grass crown, and it was the highest military honor Rome had. It could not be bought, and the Senate could not award it. It was given by an entire army to the one commander who had saved that army from destruction, and it was woven on the spot out of whatever grew on the field where the rescue happened: grass, weeds, wildflowers, whatever was underfoot. It dried out and fell apart within days. In roughly a thousand years of Roman history, fewer than ten men ever received one. A soldier who saved a single citizen's life in battle was given the corona civica, a wreath of oak leaves. Rome had more gold than it could count, and it reserved its greatest honors for objects made of plants. The value was never in the material. The value was in what the object said, and about whom. Egypt makes the opposite point. Look at any Egyptian temple wall and crowns are everywhere: the tall white crown of Upper Egypt, the red crown of Lower Egypt with its curling wire, and the double crown that fits them together to say one country, one ruler. They are carved thousands of times across three thousand years. Archaeologists have never found a single one. Not one pharaoh's crown has ever been dug up, not even from Tutankhamun's tomb, which was otherwise packed with treasure. The likeliest explanation is that they were made from leather, cloth, or reed, which rot away, and that each crown was handed to the next king rather than buried with the last one. The most famous crowns of the ancient world exist only as pictures of themselves. Medieval Europe put its argument into the shape. An open circlet, a simple ring of gold, claims that the wearer is a great person. Arches claim considerably more. When bands rise from the circlet and close over the top of the head, carrying a globe and a cross, the crown is saying that nothing and nobody sits above this ruler on earth. English kings took up the closed, arched crown around the reigns of Henry VII and Henry VIII, at precisely the moment England was insisting it owed obedience to no foreign power. The politics and the goldsmithing arrived together, which was not a coincidence. An argument that can be made can also be refused. In 1649 Parliament executed Charles I and then dealt with his crowns. The regalia was taken from Westminster Abbey, broken up, and melted into coin, and the gems were weighed and sold. The money was modest and the money was not the reason. The objects were claims, and the claims were being denied in the most physical way available. Almost nothing survived. The Coronation Spoon, silver-gilt and made in the 1100s, slipped through only because a man bought it and quietly handed it back eleven years later when the monarchy returned. Everything in the Tower of London that looks medieval was made in 1661, in a hurry, to replace what had been destroyed. Some arguments are still running. The Koh-i-Noor diamond, 105.6 carats, sits in a crown made for the Queen Mother in 1937. It was taken from a ten year old Sikh maharaja in the Punjab in 1849, under a treaty signed after a war he had lost. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Afghanistan have all asked for it back. Britain has kept it. When people argue about that diamond, they are not arguing about carbon. They are arguing about what the object claims, and whether the claim is honest. That is what a crown has always been. Not a hat. A statement, worn where everyone can see it, made in a material chosen to keep the statement hard to ignore.
